ghola.modulesDir.description: Optional override for the Ghola modules directory. By default modules are loaded from the installed extension itself. Set an absolute path, or a path relative to the workspace root, to load modules from a custom location.

ghola.cliCommand.description: LEGACY CLI-binary setting, superseded by the ghola.cliAliases registry plus ghola.selectedAlias. This value is inert unless ghola.selectedAlias is blank: whenever selectedAlias is non-empty — and it defaults to 'claude' — the alias name wins and this setting is never read. There is no longer a UI control for it; only hand-editing settings.json reaches it. When it IS in effect, the value is sent as a shell command before the Initiation Command, so the CLI starts first and the Initiation Command can be delivered to it as user input rather than as a shell command. Blank this AND ghola.selectedAlias to skip launching a CLI and send the Initiation Command directly to the shell instead.

ghola.sessionCommand.description: Initiation Command — the WORD or PHRASE sent as user input to the running CLI after it boots (NOT a shell command). The CLI's own configuration (e.g. Claude's CLAUDE.md or user memory) defines what this trigger word does — typically reading the composed TPM prompt from $GHOLA_TPM_PROMPT_FILE and adopting the TPM role. Sent ~3s after the CLI launches so the CLI has time to become ready for input. Leave empty to skip auto-sending the trigger word.

ghola.cliAliases.description: Registry of named Claude CLI aliases managed by Ghola. Each entry is { alias, command } — the alias name (e.g. "claude-1") and the shell command it expands to (e.g. "CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=$HOME/.claude command claude"). Saving this list writes a Ghola-managed block to ghola.aliasFile (default ~/.bashrc) so the aliases are available in any new shell, and exposes the alias names in the Sessions tab dropdown for one-click selection. Edit entries here or via the Sessions tab; both surfaces stay in sync.

ghola.aliasFile.description: Shell rc file where Ghola writes the managed alias block for ghola.cliAliases. Supports a leading "~" or "~/" which expands to the current user's home directory. Content outside Ghola's sentinel markers is preserved verbatim — only the block between "# >>> ghola-managed-aliases >>>" and "# <<< ghola-managed-aliases <<<" is rewritten. Point this at a different file (e.g. ~/.zshrc, ~/.bash_aliases) if your interactive shell sources aliases from somewhere other than ~/.bashrc.

ghola.selectedAlias.description: PRIMARY launch setting: the name of the alias from ghola.cliAliases that the Sessions tab launches as the CLI command. The alias name (not its expansion) is sent to the terminal so the shell's alias lookup resolves it. Defaults to 'claude', which matches the alias shipped by default in ghola.cliAliases. Whenever this is non-empty it overrides the legacy ghola.cliCommand — so on a default install cliCommand is never consulted. Deliberately blanking this field is the only way to fall back to ghola.cliCommand.

enumDescriptions: Normal manual approval — Claude Code prompts for each action. No launch flag is added.
Skip ALL permission prompts for the session (--dangerously-skip-permissions). Most permissive; a few circuit breakers (e.g. rm -rf /) still fire.
ghola.permissionMode.description: Permission mode the Ghola Session launches Claude Code in, so you do not have to press Shift+Tab. Maps to a Claude Code launch flag (see per-value descriptions). Under bypassPermissions the flag is added whenever Ghola can identify the launch command as Claude Code — either by resolving a registered ghola.cliAliases entry to a binary named 'claude', or, failing that, by the command string itself containing 'claude'. When the command cannot be identified, the flag is still appended if you set this setting explicitly (logged as best-effort, since a non-Claude binary may reject it); if it is merely sitting at its packaged default, the flag is skipped and Ghola shows a warning telling you how to fix it. Defaults to bypassPermissions (--dangerously-skip-permissions).

ghola.remoteControl.markdownDeprecationMessage: RETIRED and INERT. Remote Control is now mandatory: Ghola no longer reads this setting, so leaving it at `false` does NOT turn Remote Control off. The property is retained only so an existing `ghola.remoteControl` line in settings.json keeps validating instead of being flagged as an unknown setting — nothing reads it, and you can delete the line whenever you like. Everything Remote Control still exposes now lives on `#ghola.remoteControlSessionName#`.
ghola.remoteControl.markdownDescription: RETIRED and INERT — Remote Control is always on and this setting is never read. See `#ghola.remoteControlSessionName#`.

ghola.remoteControlSessionName.markdownDeprecationMessage: RETIRED and INERT. The Remote Control session name is now derived automatically at launch from the workspace identity, falling back to the git branch and then the workspace directory name; Ghola no longer reads this value, whether it is left empty or set. The property is retained only so an existing `ghola.remoteControlSessionName` line in settings.json keeps validating instead of being flagged as an unknown setting — nothing reads it, and you can delete the line whenever you like.
ghola.remoteControlSessionName.markdownDescription:
RETIRED — this value is no longer read (see the deprecation notice). It is kept here as the canonical reference for how Remote Control's launch mechanics work.

Ghola ALWAYS launches with Remote Control (`--remote-control <name>`), so you can steer the running local session from your phone or from claude.ai/code; it does not conflict with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. There is no toggle — the flag is appended to every session launch, and it is accepted and non-fatal even on a machine where Remote Control cannot actually come up. Ghola always passes an explicit name because `--remote-control` takes an OPTIONAL value, and an omitted name would swallow the Initiation Command as the session name.

The session name comes from a candidate chain, tried in order until one survives normalization: first the environment-qualified workspace identity — the same name the Team Switchboard roster and the VS Code status-bar pill show, e.g. `Ghola` in WSL or `cmms1@win` on native Windows — because that qualifier is what keeps two clones of the same repo running in different environments from colliding under one name, something the branch alone cannot do (several clones can share the same branch, e.g. `main`). When no workspace folder is open and that identity is unavailable, next is the current git branch of the session's working directory. After that, the working directory's own folder name. Last is the hardcoded fallback `ghola-session`, reached only when every earlier candidate comes up empty. This still beats letting the CLI generate a name on its own: Claude Code's own `--remote-control-session-name-prefix` defaults to the hostname, which makes every session on one machine look alike.

The resulting name is normalized before it is passed: whitespace and path separators become `-`, leading dashes are dropped (a name starting with `-` would be parsed as another option), and it is capped at 80 characters. If normalization leaves nothing, Ghola falls back to the repository folder name and then to `ghola-session`, so the name is never empty — an empty name would let Claude Code bind the Initiation Command as the session name and the session would boot un-initiated.

**Ghola pre-flights what it can see** and warns without ever blocking the launch: Remote Control is disabled outright when `DISABLE_TELEMETRY`, `DO_NOT_TRACK`, `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC`, or `DISABLE_GROWTHBOOK` is set in the session's environment, or when `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` points at a non-Anthropic host. Each warning names the variable and the layer it is set in — the environment VS Code started in, `terminal.integrated.env.<platform>`, or a `VAR=` prefix on the selected CLI alias — because that is the only actionable part; the session launches regardless.

**Not observable from here, so Ghola cannot check it:** Remote Control also requires a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan authenticated through OAuth (an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` will not do) and, on Team and Enterprise, the organization-level Remote Control toggle. If none of Ghola's warnings fire and Remote Control still does not come up, it is one of those.

ghola.swe.performanceCores.description: SWE performance cores (primary workers for the critical-path task).

ghola.swe.performanceCoresModel.description: Claude model used by default when SWE-class subagents are deployed onto performance cores. Performance cores handle the critical-path task; defaulting to Opus matches the highest-difficulty work this tier typically takes on. TPM may still deviate per task — this is the default, not a hard lock.

ghola.swe.efficiencyCoresModel.description: Claude model used by default when SWE-class subagents are deployed onto efficiency cores. Efficiency cores handle lower-priority side work; defaulting to Sonnet keeps cost and latency low for routine tasks. TPM may still deviate per task.

ghola.qa.model.description: Claude model used by default when QA subagents are deployed. QA verifies code changes through targeted reviews; defaulting to Sonnet matches medium-difficulty correctness work. TPM may still deviate per task — this is the default, not a hard lock.

ghola.newModulePrompt.description: Instruction text copied to clipboard when 'Copy Module Generation Instruction' is clicked in the Modules tab. Edit this to customize the instructions given to an AI agent for generating new Ghola modules.
ghola.newModulePrompt.default:
Generate a complete Ghola module ready for upload. Output the full folder contents — one manifest.json and one or more .md content files — saved to my Downloads folder under a folder named tool.<short-id>/.

The module manifest must follow this schema:

{
  "id": "tool.<short-id>",
  "name": "<Human Readable Name>",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "One concise sentence describing what this module does.",
  "proactive": false,
  "contributes": {
    "promptFragments": [
      { "target": "all", "contentPath": "<file>.md" }
    ],
    "settings": {
      "<setting-key>": {
        "type": "string",
        "label": "<UI label>",
        "description": "<2-4 sentence consequence-focused description of what each value means and what changing it does>",
        "default": "<default value>"
      }
    }
  }
}

Rules:
- target is one of: "tpm", "swe", "qa", or "all". Use "all" only when the content applies identically to every agent.
- Decide whether the module should be proactive: true or proactive: false before finalizing the manifest. Proactive modules run at session start — their content is consulted before the agent responds to the user's first request. Typical session-start work includes environment checks (e.g. WSL fast-path detection), pre-flight advisories, discovery routines (e.g. locating a configured resource), credential or connectivity validation, and banner/orientation prompts the agent should emit on first response. Default to proactive: false: most modules' content is read on demand when their domain comes up in the work and do not need to fire at session start — setting proactive: true adds noise to every session's opening flow when the module's behavior is not session-start-shaped. Set proactive: true only when both of these are true: (a) the module has work that must happen before the agent responds to the user's first request, AND (b) skipping that work would degrade the rest of the session rather than just being a missed convenience. Precedents (proactive: true): tool.fastpath-check fires at session start because the WSL fast-path warning must appear before the user starts working in a slow path; tool.obsidian-notes fires at session start because vault discovery must resolve a path before any notes operation can happen this session. Anti-precedents (proactive: false): tool.git, tool.dotnet-suite, tool.database-access, tool.npm-suite, and tool.lenses are all proactive: false because their content only matters when their domain (git commands, dotnet commands, DB queries, allowlisted npm/Angular commands, review/planning mode) comes up — never at session start.
- Content .md files contain agent instructions, rules, or capability descriptions.
- Settings descriptions must explain consequences — what each value means in practice, what changing it does at runtime, default rationale.
- The module-level description must be ONE sentence.
- When writing descriptions (both module-level and per-setting), do NOT use backticks anywhere — descriptions are rendered as plain text and backticks appear literally rather than as styled code. Use plain words, double-quotes for ambiguous literals, or rephrase to avoid the need.
- Setting label fields must use Title Case — capitalize every word's first letter (e.g. "Fast Path Directory", "Workspace Repository Resolution"). This matches the panel's house style.
- Set fullWidth: true on any field that renders a table — keyValue fields (kv-table) and fields that declare a keywordsPath (keywords reference table) — so the table fills the settings panel width instead of capping at 720px. Place it at the end of the field object after keyLabel/valueLabel/optionalEnabled/optionalDescription. Precedent: tool.database-access, tool.dotnet-suite, tool.git.
- On a keyValue field whose value column represents a small fixed taxonomy (e.g. a permission category like r/w/d), set valueReadonly: true so existing rows render as styled non-editable text rather than an editable input — this prevents users from typing arbitrary values. Precedent: tool.git's allowedCommands field with its r|w|d Category column.
- Whenever valueReadonly: true is set and the value column has a fixed enumerable set of allowed values, also set valueOptions: [...]. The add-new-entry row then renders a select dropdown populated from these options so users can still add rows via the UI. Precedent: tool.git's allowedCommands has valueOptions: ["r", "w", "d"].
- Default to native checkboxes for kv-table Enabled columns. When optionalEnabled: true is set the Enabled column renders as a native checkbox automatically; do NOT add enabledStyle unless you specifically want the .switch/.slider toggle pattern, in which case set enabledStyle: "toggle". Toggles are intentionally avoided for table Enabled columns project-wide. Precedent: tool.npm-suite's allowedCommands.
- When a keywordsPath field's domain has a clearer collective noun than "Keywords" (e.g. "Functions", "Commands"), set keywordsLabel to override the reference table's subtitle. When the same field is also multiSelect: true and the override more naturally describes the toggle action (e.g. "Enabled" for an allowlist), set selectColumnLabel to override the leading checkbox column header. Both default to "Keywords"/"Select" — only override when there is a genuine semantic improvement. Precedent: tool.dotnet-suite's allowedCommands uses "Functions"/"Enabled".

UI styling standards (when extending the panel or designing settings):

- Centering action icons in a kv-table cell requires the CSS selector ".kv-table .kv-cell-actions" with the ".kv-table" ancestor. A loose ".kv-cell-actions" selector loses specificity to the base ".kv-table td" rule and the icon ends up left-aligned.
- Inputs in a kv-table add-row use class "kv-input" and auto-render at 28px height with VS Code input theming. The Add button uses class "kv-add-button" which is also 28px. Do not manually tweak heights — these two classes already match.
- kv-table CSS rules must be globally scoped, never nested under ".module-detail". The same kv-table pattern is reused in the Sessions tab outside ".module-detail" context. When adding a new kv-* rule, omit the ".module-detail" prefix unless the rule is specific to the module-detail view.
- Editable fields auto-save on commit. String, number, and enum fields listen for the "change" event (fires on blur for inputs, on selection for selects) and call persistSettings() directly. Do not add a manual save button.
- For one-off layout tweaks (tightening the gap between a heading and its description, etc.), use inline styles via element.style or the el() helper's style attribute. Reserve new CSS rules for patterns that will recur.
- Reuse the existing class kit before inventing new classes. Available: kv-table, kv-table-wrap, kv-row, kv-cell, kv-cell-key, kv-cell-actions, kv-cell-enabled, kv-input, kv-add-cell, kv-add-field, kv-add-label, kv-add-button, kv-delete-button, kv-empty-row, kv-add-foot, kv-add-row, icon-button, icon-button.framed, primary, secondary, setting-input, setting-label, setting-desc, setting-keywords-heading, subtitle, section-divider.

ghola.repoPath.description: Absolute path to your Project-Ghola git clone, used by 'Ghola: Update Extension' to locate the source checkout to pull, rebuild, and reinstall. Resolution order: this setting, when it names a directory containing '.git'; then the extension's own install path, if that path holds both '.git' and 'esbuild.config.js' (the F5 dev host or a source install); then the first open workspace folder verified as a genuine Ghola clone ('.git' plus 'esbuild.config.js' plus a package.json whose name is 'ghola'). Set this when running from an installed VSIX without your clone open, or to force the update to come from one specific clone. On a native-Windows host where none of those resolve, a POSIX-absolute value here (one starting with a single '/' — a '//server/share' UNC spelling is deliberately excluded) is instead read as evidence that the clone lives inside WSL and the update is delegated there: Ghola picks the distribution by probing each installed one for the repo's '.git', runs that checkout's own scripts/reinstall.sh inside it, and installs the resulting vsix from the Windows side.

ghola.linqpadConnectionsPath.description: Absolute path to LINQPad's ConnectionsV2.xml file. When set, Ghola uses this path verbatim instead of probing common Windows/WSL locations. Leave empty for the default discovery order: $APPDATA/LINQPad/ConnectionsV2.xml, then /mnt/c/Users/$USER/AppData/Roaming/LINQPad/ConnectionsV2.xml, then iteration over /mnt/c/Users/* profiles, then a wslvar USERPROFILE fallback. Changing this value re-probes immediately and re-broadcasts the resulting connection list to any open Ghola settings panel.

ghola.linqpadInstallPrompt.description: Instruction text copied to clipboard when the 'Copy install instructions' button is clicked on the LINQPad-not-installed banner in the Modules tab. Edit this to customize the instructions given to an AI assistant for walking a user through installing LINQPad and exporting their connection metadata so Ghola's Database Access module can populate its connection allowlist.
ghola.linqpadInstallPrompt.default:
I need to install LINQPad on Windows and create at least one named connection so the Ghola VS Code extension can detect it.

Walk me through:

1. Where to download LINQPad for my Windows version (free edition is fine).
2. How to install it without admin rights if my machine is locked down.
3. After install, how to add a new connection — specifically a SQL Server connection. I need to enter:
   - Server name (instance form: hostname or hostname\instance)
   - Authentication (Windows Integrated vs SQL Login)
   - Database name (optional — a server-only connection is allowed)
4. Where LINQPad stores the resulting connection metadata. Confirm it is at %APPDATA%\LINQPad\ConnectionsV2.xml and explain how to verify that file exists.
5. If I am running VS Code under WSL, how to make sure the WSL side can read the Windows-side ConnectionsV2.xml (the default /mnt/c/Users/<me>/AppData/Roaming/LINQPad/ path).

Keep the steps short and actionable. I will paste your reply into a notes app and follow it linearly.

ghola.statusBar.enabled.description: Show the Ghola status-bar item, whose label takes the shape 'Ghola: <identity> · <modality> · <tokens> · 5h <percent>%' — the literal 'Ghola:' prefix, then this window's Team Switchboard identity, this session's modality, and the context-size and 5-hour-usage segments reported for this instance, joined by ' · ' — e.g. 'Ghola: cmms2@win · Ticket Work · 262k · 5h 40%' — with a flame icon in place of the org icon while War Mode is on. The 'Ghola:' prefix and the modality always render; the identity segment is omitted entirely when no workspace folder is open and no identity resolves, with no placeholder and no fallback literal; the two usage segments appear only while a live Claude Code session is writing state for this instance. That identity appears in both the label and the hover tooltip, and is derived from the git repository root at or above the first open workspace folder, with a leading 'Project-' stripped and an environment qualifier appended on every host except WSL, which holds the unqualified name ('@win', '@mac'); it is always derived and is not overridable. Clicking the item opens Ghola's settings panel.

scripts.dev: concurrently --kill-others-on-fail --names build,extension --prefix-colors yellow,cyan "npm:watch" "echo Press F5 in VS Code to launch the Extension Development Host"
scripts.package: npm run build && vsce package -o ghola.vsix
